unit-phys-dyn1-newton.title: Dynamics 1 · 1-1 Forces and Newton’s Laws
unit-phys-dyn1-newton.srcName: Chapter 6, Forces (6.1 Force and Motion, 6.3 Interaction Forces)

summary.text: What a force is and where forces come from: systems and their environment, contact and long-range forces, naming the agent of every force, free-body diagrams, adding forces to get the net force, and Newton’s three laws — the second as F_net = ma, the first as the law of inertia and equilibrium, and the third as forces that always come in pairs on two different objects. Tension in ropes and the four fundamental forces round it off.

why.text: Kinematics described motion without asking what caused it. This is the cause. Every problem in the rest of the course — slopes, circles, energy, collisions — starts with the same move: find every force on one object, add them, and let the net force set the acceleration.

objectives.text: Define a force and differentiate between contact forces and long-range forces.
Recognise the significance of Newton’s second law of motion and use it to solve motion problems.
Explain the meaning of Newton’s first law and describe an object in equilibrium.
Explain the meaning of interaction pairs of forces and how they are related by Newton’s third law.
Explain the tension in ropes and strings in terms of Newton’s third law.

parentNote.text: The first part of the new Dynamics 1 shelf, from chapter 6.1 (Force and Motion) and 6.3 (Interaction Forces) of the textbook pages in the Dynamics 1 folder. No objective sheet was in the folder, so the objectives above are the chapter’s own. Every number was computed with sympy in the builder and checked before it was written, and none of the chapter’s worked-example numbers is reused. Four misconceptions get deliberate airtime because the chapter names them and they cost marks quietly: that a moving object needs a net force to keep moving (it needs one only to CHANGE its motion — the constant-speed crate question offers "the pull must win" as a wrong answer); that the thrower’s force travels with the ball; that a third-law pair can cancel (it acts on two different objects, so it never can — the book-on-a-table question is the classic test of this); and that any single force, rather than the net force, sets the acceleration. The tug-of-war tension trap (450 N, not 900 N) is in too. No free-body diagrams are drawn in the app: its graph engine draws gridded plots with plain lines and no arrowheads, so an "arrow" would really be a line on graph paper and could mislead more than help. Every force is described in words instead, and the chapter asks her to draw these diagrams by hand, which is the better practice anyway.

nextUp.text: Read the cards on the three laws until you can say each one without looking, then take the quiz. For every question, name each force by its agent before you calculate anything.

cards.def:
**A force is a push or a pull exerted on an object.**
• It has a size and a direction, so it is a vector.
• It is measured in newtons (N).

**The system is the object you are studying; the environment is everything around it that can push or pull on it.**
• Draw a circle round the system and look for every place the environment touches it. Contact forces act at exactly those places.

**A contact force acts only by touching; a long-range force acts without any contact at all.**
• Contact: a hand, a rope, a floor, friction, air pushing on you.
• Long-range: gravity (and magnets). In this unit gravity is the only long-range force in play.

**Every real force has a specific thing exerting it, called its agent — if you cannot name the agent, the force does not exist.**
• Name forces as "agent on object": the rope on the bucket, Earth on the ball.
• This one rule kills most invented forces, including "the force of the throw" after the ball has left the hand.
cards.hint: No agent, no force. Ask "what is doing the pushing?"

cards.def:
**A free-body diagram replaces the object with a dot and draws every force on it as an arrow with its tail on the dot.**
• Arrow length shows the size of the force; arrow direction shows its direction.
• Only forces ON the object belong there — never forces the object exerts on something else.
• Draw these by hand on paper; the app describes them in words.

**The net force is the vector sum of every force acting on the object.**
• Same direction: add. Opposite directions: subtract, and the net points the way of the bigger one.
• At right angles: combine with Pythagoras, then find the angle with tan⁻¹ — exactly as you did with vectors in Kinematics 2.

**The acceleration of an object is the net force on it divided by its mass, and it points the same way as the net force.**
• Bigger net force, bigger acceleration. Bigger mass, smaller acceleration.
• It is the NET force that goes in, never just one of the forces.

**One newton is the net force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².**
• So 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².
• For scale, a medium apple weighs about 1 N.

**An object at rest stays at rest, and a moving object keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed, if and only if the net force on it is zero.**
• A net force does not keep things moving. It CHANGES how they are moving.

**Inertia is an object’s tendency to resist a change in its velocity.**
• The more mass, the more inertia.
• Inertia is not a force. It is a property of the object, so it never appears as an arrow on a free-body diagram.

**An object is in equilibrium when the net force on it is zero — which means it is either at rest OR moving at constant velocity.**
• Being at rest is just the special case of constant velocity where the velocity happens to be zero.
• Equilibrium does not mean "no forces". It means the forces cancel.

cards.term: Moving does not need a net force
cards.def:
**A force is needed to CHANGE motion, not to keep it going.**
• A crate pulled at constant speed has a pull exactly equal to the friction — not bigger. If the pull were bigger, the crate would be speeding up.
• On a frictionless surface, a sliding object needs no forward force at all to keep sliding.
cards.hint: Constant velocity always means balanced, however fast it is going.

cards.term: The throw does not travel with the ball
cards.def:
**Once a thrown ball leaves the hand, the hand’s force is gone.**
• A hand is a contact force, and contact has been broken.
• Ignoring air, the only force left on the ball is gravity. It keeps moving forward because nothing is stopping it, not because something is pushing it.

**ma is what the net force equals, not an extra force of its own.**
• Experiments show the two sides of F_net = ma are equal; the equals sign does not create a new arrow.
• Never draw an "ma" arrow on a free-body diagram.

**Forces come in pairs: if A pushes on B, then B pushes on A with a force of equal size in the opposite direction.**
• The two forces act on DIFFERENT objects.
• Neither one causes the other. They exist together or not at all.

**The two forces in a third-law pair act on different objects, so they can never cancel each other out.**
• Forces only cancel when they act on the SAME object.
• A book on a table: the table’s push up and Earth’s pull down are equal and opposite, but both act on the book, so they are NOT a pair. The partner of Earth pulling the book is the book pulling Earth.
cards.hint: Swap the names. The partner of "A on B" is always "B on A".

cards.term: What actually pushes a car forward
cards.def:
**The road pushes the car forward.**
• The tyres push backwards on the road; by the third law the road pushes forwards on the tyres with the same size of force.
• That is why a car cannot accelerate on ice — no grip, no forward push from the road.

cards.term: Earth moves too, but not much
cards.def:
**When a ball falls, it pulls up on Earth exactly as hard as Earth pulls down on it — but Earth’s enormous mass makes its acceleration unmeasurably small.**
• Same force, wildly different masses, so wildly different accelerations: a = F_net / m on each.

**Tension is the pull a taut rope exerts, and in a light rope it is the same all the way along.**
• In a tug-of-war where each team pulls with 400 N and nothing moves, the tension is 400 N — not 800 N.
• Each end of the rope is just the other end’s third-law partner.

**Physicists recognise four fundamental interactions: gravitational, electromagnetic, strong nuclear and weak nuclear.**
• Every contact force — friction, the normal force, tension — is electromagnetic underneath.
• The two nuclear forces act inside the nucleus of an atom.

questions.q: Which of these is a long-range force?
opts: Gravity pulling on a falling apple
Friction from a carpet on a sliding box
The tension in a rope lifting a bucket
The push of a table holding up a book
questions.hint: Which one acts without anything touching?
steps: A contact force needs the agent to touch the object.
Friction, tension and a table’s push all need contact.
Gravity acts across empty space between the apple and Earth.
Gravity is the long-range force.

ex.main: **Gravity is the only one here that acts without touching.** Friction, tension and a supporting surface all work through contact, which is why the circle-the-system step finds them at the touch points.
ex.tip: Look for the touch points first; whatever is left over is long-range.

questions.q: What does it mean for an object to be in equilibrium?
opts: No forces of any kind are acting on it at that moment
The net force on it is zero, so it is at rest or at constant velocity
It is at rest, and only being at rest counts as equilibrium
Its speed is constant, though it may be changing direction
questions.hint: Equilibrium is about the NET force.
steps: Equilibrium is defined by the net force being zero.
Zero net force means no acceleration.
No acceleration means constant velocity, and rest is the special case of zero velocity.
So it is at rest or moving at constant velocity.

ex.main: **Zero net force — which allows rest or steady straight-line motion.** Plenty of forces can act, as long as they cancel. A steady speed while turning is NOT equilibrium, because a change of direction is an acceleration.

questions.q: Two people push a stalled car in opposite directions along a level road: one with 310 N east, the other with 190 N west. What is the net force from the two of them?
opts: 120 N west
500 N east
120 N east
500 N west
steps: The forces point in opposite directions, so subtract the sizes.
The net force points the way of the larger force, east.
The net force is 120 N east.

ex.main: **Opposite forces subtract: 310 − 190 = 120 N, pointing east because the east push is bigger.** 500 N is what you would get adding them, which only applies when both push the same way.
ex.tip: A net force always has a direction. Say it.

questions.q: A sled is pulled with 120 N toward the north and 160 N toward the east at the same time. What is the net force on it?
opts: 40 N, 53.1° east of north
280 N, 53.1° east of north
200 N, 36.9° east of north
200 N, 53.1° east of north
questions.hint: The two pulls are at right angles.
steps: Perpendicular forces combine with Pythagoras.
Measured from north, tan θ = 160 ÷ 120, so θ = 53.1° toward the east.
The net force is 200 N, 53.1° east of north.

ex.main: **√(120² + 160²) = 200 N, at tan⁻¹(160 ÷ 120) = 53.1° east of north.** 280 N adds forces at right angles as if they were in a line, and 36.9° is the right angle measured from the wrong axis — it is 36.9° north of east, not east of north.
ex.tip: Name the axis you measured from, or the angle means nothing.

questions.q: A 1350 kg car’s engine drives it forward with 3600 N while friction and air drag push back with 900 N in total. What is its acceleration?
opts: 2.0 m/s²
2.7 m/s²
3.3 m/s²
questions.hint: Which force goes into F_net = ma?
steps: Find the net force first: 3600 N forward − 900 N back = 2700 N forward.
Then a = F_net / m.
a = 2.0 m/s², forward.

ex.main: **Acceleration comes from the NET force: (3600 − 900) ÷ 1350 = 2.0 m/s².** 2.7 m/s² uses the engine force on its own, which is the commonest error in the topic; 3.3 m/s² adds the drag instead of subtracting it; 0.50 m/s² divides the mass by the force.
ex.tip: Net force in, acceleration out. Never one force on its own.

questions.q: A 2.4 N net force gives cart A an acceleration of 0.60 m/s². The same 2.4 N net force gives cart B an acceleration of 1.8 m/s². What is cart B’s mass?
opts: 4.0 kg
1.3 kg
12 kg
questions.hint: Three times the acceleration from the same force — what does that say about mass?
steps: Cart A: m = F_net / a = 2.4 ÷ 0.60 = 4.0 kg.
B accelerates three times as much, so it has one third of A’s mass.
Cart B’s mass is 1.3 kg.

ex.main: **Same force, three times the acceleration, so one third of the mass: 2.4 ÷ 1.8 = 1.3 kg.** 4.0 kg is cart A’s mass, 12 kg runs the ratio the wrong way, and 0.75 kg divides the acceleration by the force.
ex.tip: For a fixed force, mass and acceleration go opposite ways.

questions.q: A rope pulls a crate across a rough floor at a constant 1.5 m/s with a horizontal force of 85 N. How big is the friction force on the crate?
opts: More than 85 N — friction always beats a pull
Less than 85 N — the pull must win to keep it going
85 N — at constant speed the forces balance
Zero — friction stops acting once a crate moves
questions.hint: What does constant speed in a straight line tell you about the net force?
steps: Constant velocity means zero acceleration.
By the first law, zero acceleration means zero net force.
The only horizontal forces are the 85 N pull and friction, so they must cancel.
Friction is 85 N, opposite the pull.

ex.main: **Constant velocity means zero net force, so friction exactly matches the 85 N pull.** The idea that the pull must "win" to keep the crate moving is the misconception Newton’s first law exists to correct: if the pull won, the crate would be speeding up.
ex.tip: Steady and straight means balanced, however fast it is going.

questions.q: A hockey puck glides across perfectly frictionless ice in a straight line at constant speed. Which horizontal forces act on it?
opts: A small forward force that matches its speed
The stick’s push, still acting from the hit
A forward force of inertia carrying it
None — nothing is needed to keep it moving
questions.hint: Name the agent of each force offered.
steps: On frictionless ice nothing touches the puck sideways.
The stick lost contact after the hit, so its force is gone.
Inertia is a property of the puck, not a force with an agent.
So no horizontal force acts, and by the first law its velocity stays the same.

ex.main: **No horizontal force acts, and none is needed: with zero net force a moving object keeps its velocity.** The stick’s force ended with contact, and inertia is not a force — it has no agent, so it cannot appear on a free-body diagram.
ex.tip: If you cannot name the agent, the force is not there.

questions.q: A book rests on a table. The table pushes up on the book and Earth pulls down on the book, with forces of equal size. Are these two forces a Newton’s third-law pair?
opts: No — both act on the book, so they are not a pair
Yes — they are equal in size and opposite in direction
Yes — one is the reaction caused by the other one
No — third-law pairs only happen when things move
questions.hint: A third-law pair is "A on B" and "B on A". Check the objects.
steps: The table’s push is the table on the book.
The gravity force is Earth on the book.
Both act on the same object, the book, so they cannot be a pair.
They balance because of the first law; the partner of Earth-on-book is book-on-Earth.

ex.main: **Not a pair: a third-law pair acts on two DIFFERENT objects, and both of these act on the book.** They are equal because the book is in equilibrium, which is a first-law fact. The true partners are the book pulling up on Earth and the book pushing down on the table.
ex.tip: Swap the two names: the partner of A-on-B is B-on-A.

questions.q: A horse pulls on a cart, and the cart pulls back on the horse with a force of exactly the same size. How can the cart ever start moving?
opts: It cannot — the two equal pulls cancel, so neither one moves at all
Only forces ON the cart decide its motion, and the pull can beat friction
The horse must pull a little harder than the cart pulls back on it
The horse’s pull happens first, before the cart has time to pull back
questions.hint: Which object does each of the two forces act on?
steps: The horse-on-cart pull acts on the cart; the cart-on-horse pull acts on the horse.
Forces on different objects never cancel.
To see whether the cart accelerates, add only the forces on the cart: the horse’s pull forward and friction back.
If the pull is bigger than the friction, the cart accelerates.

ex.main: **The pair acts on two different objects, so it never cancels.** The cart moves if the forces ON THE CART — the horse’s pull against the ground’s friction — are unbalanced. The horse itself moves forward because the ground pushes it forward harder than the cart pulls it back.
ex.tip: Pick one object. Add only the forces on it.

questions.q: In a tug-of-war, each team pulls on its end of a rope with 450 N and the rope does not move. What is the tension in the rope?
opts: 0 N
questions.hint: Think of either end of the rope as the partner of the other.
steps: Each team pulls on the rope with 450 N.
The rope does not accelerate, so the forces on it balance.
At any point the rope is pulled 450 N each way, which is what tension measures.
The tension is 450 N.

ex.main: **The tension equals the pull at each end: 450 N.** Adding the two teams to get 900 N is the classic mistake — one team is only the third-law partner of the other end of the rope. A rope tied to a tree and pulled with 450 N has the same 450 N tension.
ex.tip: Tension is the pull at one end, not both ends added.

questions.q: A 0.25 kg ball is dropped. Earth’s mass is 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg. How big is Earth’s acceleration toward the ball while it falls?
opts: 2.4 × 10²⁴ m/s²
9.8 m/s², the same as the ball
Exactly zero — the ball pulls on nothing
questions.hint: The ball pulls Earth as hard as Earth pulls the ball.
steps: Earth pulls the ball with F = mg = 0.25 × 9.8 = 2.45 N.
By the third law, the ball pulls Earth with 2.45 N.
Earth’s acceleration is a = F_net / m = 2.45 ÷ (6.0 × 10²⁴).
a = 4.1 × 10⁻²⁵ m/s², far too small to measure.

ex.main: **The ball pulls on Earth with the same 2.45 N, but Earth’s huge mass makes the acceleration 4.1 × 10⁻²⁵ m/s².** It is not zero — the third law guarantees the force — just unmeasurable. 2.4 × 10²⁴ m/s² divides the mass by the force instead of the other way round.
ex.tip: Equal forces do not mean equal accelerations. Divide by each mass.

opts: An object’s tendency to resist any change in its velocity
A force that keeps moving objects going forward
The pull of gravity on an object, measured in newtons
The steady speed a falling object settles at
questions.hint: Is it something the object HAS, or something done TO it?
steps: A force needs an agent outside the object.
Inertia has no agent; it is a property of the object itself.
It describes how hard it is to change the object’s velocity.
Inertia is the tendency to resist a change in velocity.

ex.main: **Inertia is a property, not a force: an object’s resistance to having its velocity changed.** The pull of gravity is weight, and the steady falling speed is terminal velocity — both real, both something else.
ex.tip: Forces are done to objects. Inertia is something an object has.

questions.q: A pitcher throws a ball. Ignoring air, which forces act on the ball while it is in flight?
opts: Gravity, plus the force of the throw carrying it on
Only gravity, pulling straight down
Only the force of the throw, until it runs out
Gravity, plus a forward force from its inertia
questions.hint: Name the agent of every force you include.
steps: The hand pushed the ball only while touching it.
In flight nothing touches the ball, so there are no contact forces.
Gravity is long-range and keeps acting.
The only force in flight is gravity, downward.

ex.main: **Once contact ends, the hand’s force ends; gravity is the only force left.** The ball keeps moving forward because nothing pushes it backwards, which is the first law, not a leftover push. This is why projectiles have no horizontal acceleration.

questions.q: A car accelerates forward from a traffic light. Which force on the car actually pushes it forward?
opts: The engine’s push on the car, from inside it
The tyres’ push on the road, pointing backward
The road’s friction on the tyres, pointing forward
The car’s own momentum, building as it goes
questions.hint: For the car to accelerate, a force must act ON the car, from outside it.
steps: The tyres push backward on the road.
That force acts on the road, so it cannot accelerate the car.
By the third law, the road pushes forward on the tyres with the same size of force.
That forward push from the road is what accelerates the car.

ex.main: **The road pushes the car forward — the third-law partner of the tyres pushing the road back.** The tyres’ push acts on the road, so it is the wrong object as well as the wrong direction. Take the grip away, as on ice, and the engine can roar all it likes.
ex.tip: Ask what is pushing ON the car from outside it.

questions.q: Which fundamental force is responsible for every everyday contact force, such as friction and the push of a floor?
opts: The weak nuclear force
The gravitational force
The strong nuclear force
The electromagnetic force
questions.hint: Contact forces come from atoms pushing and pulling on atoms.
steps: Contact forces happen where the atoms of two surfaces meet.
Atoms and molecules are held together, and pushed apart, by electric forces.
The two nuclear forces act only inside the nucleus.
Contact forces are electromagnetic.

ex.main: **Every contact force is electromagnetic underneath — the electrons of two surfaces repelling and attracting.** Gravity is the long-range force in this unit, and the strong and weak forces work only inside the nucleus.
ex.tip: Touching is atoms meeting atoms, and that is electromagnetism.

questions.q: A lamp hangs at rest from a cord. Which forces belong on the lamp’s free-body diagram?
opts: The cord pulling up and gravity pulling down, equal in size
Gravity pulling down only, since the lamp is just hanging there
The cord pulling up only, since nothing about the lamp is moving
The cord up, gravity down, and the lamp pulling down on the cord
questions.hint: Only forces acting ON the lamp go on its diagram.
steps: Two agents act on the lamp: the cord touching it, and Earth.
The cord pulls up; gravity pulls down.
The lamp is at rest, so the net force is zero and the two are equal.
The lamp pulling the cord is a force ON the cord, so it stays off.

ex.main: **Tension up, gravity down, equal in size because the lamp is in equilibrium.** The lamp’s pull on the cord is a real force, but it acts on the cord, so it belongs on the cord’s diagram — never the lamp’s.
ex.tip: One diagram, one object, only the forces on it.

questions.q: A cart accelerates at 3.0 m/s² under a certain net force. The net force is doubled AND the cart’s mass is doubled. What is its new acceleration?
opts: 6.0 m/s²
3.0 m/s²
1.5 m/s²
12 m/s²
questions.hint: a = F_net / m. What happens to a fraction when top and bottom both double?
steps: Acceleration is F_net divided by m.
Doubling F_net doubles the top of the fraction.
Doubling m doubles the bottom, which cancels it.
The acceleration stays 3.0 m/s².

ex.main: **Doubling both the net force and the mass leaves a = F_net / m unchanged at 3.0 m/s².** 6.0 m/s² sees only the force, 1.5 m/s² only the mass, and 12 m/s² multiplies by both instead of dividing.
ex.tip: Change two things at once? Write the fraction and watch both.

questions.q: Rank these carts from GREATEST to LEAST acceleration.
opts: Cart A: 18 N forward on a 3.0 kg cart
Cart B: 30 N forward and 10 N back on a 4.0 kg cart
Cart C: 24 N forward on a 6.0 kg cart
Cart D: 40 N forward on a 20 kg cart
questions.hint: Find each net force before dividing by the mass.
steps: B: the net force is 30 − 10 = 20 N, so 20 ÷ 4.0 = 5.0 m/s².
So A, then B, then C, then D.

ex.main: **A (6.0), B (5.0), C (4.0), D (2.0) m/s².** Cart B is the trap: using only its 30 N forward force gives 7.5 m/s² and puts it first. And cart D has the biggest force of all but the smallest acceleration, because its mass is biggest by more.
ex.tip: Biggest force does not mean biggest acceleration. Divide.

items.t: A lamp hanging still from the ceiling
items.why: At rest, so zero acceleration and zero net force: the cord’s pull matches gravity.

items.t: A car on cruise control at a steady 100 km/h on a straight, level road
items.why: Constant speed in a straight line is constant velocity, so the net force is zero. Fast is not the same as accelerating.

items.t: A sky diver falling at a constant terminal speed
items.why: At terminal velocity the air’s drag has grown to equal her weight.

items.t: A book lying on a desk
items.why: The desk pushes up exactly as hard as gravity pulls down.

items.t: An elevator rising at a steady 2 m/s
items.why: Moving up, but not speeding up or slowing down — constant velocity, zero net force.

items.t: A puck gliding straight at constant speed on frictionless ice
items.why: Nothing acts sideways at all, and nothing needs to: the first law keeps it going.

items.t: A car pulling away from a red light
items.why: Speeding up is accelerating, so the net force points forward.

items.t: A bike braking to a stop
items.why: Slowing down is accelerating too, with the net force pointing backward.

items.t: A ball at the very top of its throw, momentarily still
items.why: Still for an instant, but gravity is the only force on it — the velocity is about to change.

items.t: A car going round a bend at a steady 40 km/h
items.why: Steady speed, but the direction is changing, and a change of direction is an acceleration.

items.t: An apple just after it leaves the branch
items.why: Only gravity acts, so it speeds up as it falls.

items.t: A rocket lifting off and gaining speed
items.why: The thrust beats its weight, so the net force points up and it accelerates.
